=== MULTI-SOURCE TOPIC CLUSTER: Conservative influencer James O’Keefe charged with unlawful voting and identity theft in Minnesota ===

[Source 1 — www.nbcnews.com] (URL: https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/james-okeefe-minnesota-unlawful-voting-identity-theft-charges-rcna606142):
Stated Claim / Post Context:
Conservative influencer James O’Keefe charged with unlawful voting and identity theft in Minnesota

O’Keefe was charged alongside fellow influencer Cam Higby. They are accused of misrepresenting themselves at polling places during Minnesota’s primary in August.

Actual Article Body:
For You

Settings

news Alerts

There are no new alerts at this time

A Minnesota prosecutor charged conservative provocateur James O’Keefe and influencer Cam Higby on Wednesday with felony counts of unlawful voting and identity theft after they showed up at polling places in August using the names of registered voters.

Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty, who announced the charges at a news conference, accused the pair of entering polling places during state primary election voting on Aug. 11 and identifying themselves using the names of registered voters in those precincts without those voters’ knowledge or permission.

Influencer James O’Keefe charged with unlawful voting

“Both men stopped short of signing the oath we all sign before receiving our ballot,” she said. “But Minnesota law states clearly that no individual shall intentionally misrepresent their identity in applying for a ballot.”

O’Keefe and Higby were using a process under Minnesota law known as vouching. It allows people to vouch for other voters on Election Day. A registered voter who lives in the same precinct can vouch for up to eight voters, while staff members of residential facilities can vouch for their residents.

The pair of influencers disguised and recorded themselves going undercover using hidden cameras at the polling places. They posted videos capturing their interactions on social media in August. O’Keefe said on X that they dressed in “Muslim garb” — including, for one of them, a full-face veil known as a niqab — and that their goal was to “expose the sheer lunacy of Minnesota’s ‘vouching’ system.”

Moriarty said Wednesday the office of Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon alerted her office to their conduct.

After O’Keefe and Higby’s videos became public in August, Simon said in a statement that their “apparent goal was to cast doubt on one or more Minnesota election laws that have been in force for over fifty years. Instead, they revealed their ignorance of how those laws actually work — while putting themselves in legal jeopardy.”

“The misconduct by this group is outrageous and totally unacceptable,” Simon added. “We have zero tolerance for lying, lawbreaking, and disruptions at our polling places.”

Police interviewed the registered voters whose names O’Keefe and Higby used, said Moriarty, who added that they also used the names of deceased voters. Asked where they obtained those names, Moriarty said, “We don’t know that.”

Moriarty said that they are not in jail and that instead, they will be issued summonses to appear in court in Minnesota.

Neither O’Keefe nor Higby immediately responded to requests for comment.

President Donald Trump has alleged for years that Democrats have committed voter fraud or have rigged elections against him. As part of those efforts to crack down on and prevent purported voter fraud, the Trump administration has been targeting Democratic-controlled states by trying to obtain state voter roll lists and identifying alleged noncitizen voters.

O’Keefe has been involved in other voter fraud-related incidents. In 2024, he and Project Veritas, which he founded, settled a lawsuit brought by a Pennsylvania postmaster after the group promoted a postal worker’s false claims of voter fraud during the 2020 presidential election. O’Keefe was removed as the head of Project Veritas in 2023.

Higby was a journalist for conservative outlets and now operates a YouTube account with 285,000 subscribers.

Rebecca Shabad is a politics reporter for NBC News based in Washington.

Actual Article Body:
Evidence suggesting Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., married her brother goes back at least to 2016, when the Obama administration opened an investigation into the alleged marital and immigration fraud. Republican Minnesota State Rep. Kristin Robbins said everyone in her state knew about it the whole time.

“This has been an open secret in Minnesota for many years,” Robbins, chairwoman of the House Fraud Prevention and State Oversight Committee, told The Federalist. “Everyone here has heard it and was not surprised by it.”

But while “Democrats felt it was just a political smear job by the Republicans, and most Republicans thought it was true,” many of those who believed it was true “decided speaking out wasn’t worth it” because “anyone who raised it was called a racist and an Islamophobe.”

“Every time someone said there was fraud in the Somali community, whether it was a politician or a whistleblower inside the agencies, they were called racist, they were called Islamophobic,” Robbins said. “In many cases, the whistleblowers were required to go to DEI training if they said anything.”

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and Department of Homeland Security (DHS) opened the investigation into Omar, whose real name, federal officials believe, is Ilhan Nur Said Elmi. According to The New York Times, current and former officials say there was evidence at the time that her marriage to Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, a man believed to be her brother, was fraudulent. Ahmed currently writes about his experience as a “gay man of the East African diaspora” living as an academic in the United Kingdom.

Robbins said that one “stunning development” that came out was the use of the Nur Said Elmi name, because Ilhan had always presented her last name as “Omar.” The discrepancy stems from evidence suggesting Elmi’s father — through whom she obtained her citizenship in 2000, purportedly as a minor child — assumed a different identity as well in order to claim refugee status.

Elmi’s citizenship itself is under scrutiny due to possible immigration fraud separate from the marriage to her brother, as it appears she was an adult at the time she obtained it, despite claiming to be a minor.

But Robbins wants to know if there was foul play on the part of the Obama administration to cover for Omar as she became prominent in Minnesota, and then national politics.

“If the Obama administration was looking into this, did they slow walk it so that the statute of limitations ran out?” she asked. “When did they start investigating it? And how long did it take them to conclude that it was too late to do anything?”

Elmi’s fraudulent marriage was reported by Alpha News and Power Line about 10 years ago. Alpha News says a letter from then-Minnesota U.S. Attorney Andrew Luger “helped quiet allegations” that Elmi “married her brother in an immigration fraud scheme.”

Today, Luger claims that the letter  “was never meant to say anything about the substance of the claims.”

According to New York Times reporting, two officials confirmed that Ahmed was given a provisional green card for two years, by way of his marriage to Ilhan. After officials asked for more information about the marriage, Ahmed fled the country.

In 2016, there was also a local Fox affiliate article related to questions over Elmi’s marriages, which was subsequently taken off the internet. However, part of the article is still available and states, “We aren’t the only ones who still have questions about the two men the DFL-endorsed House candidate has called her husband, without divorcing either.”

Actual Article Body:
An illegal immigrant running from Canadian prosecutors was arrested in September after allegedly trying to recruit as a fake CIA official in the United States, newly unsealed court records show.

An Oct. 7 indictment in Georgia accuses Lakotah Salvini of leading a fraudulent “intelligence” organization called Castle International with co-defendant Richard Myers since at least December 2025. The pair advertised their fake services to a sheriff’s deputy, tried to approach a Navy base in Georgia, and may have recruited an unnamed Pentagon employee, the Department of Justice claimed.
